title: Infectious Disease and the Immune System
seo_title: Year 12 Biology: Infectious Disease and Immunity Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Pathogens (viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists, parasites, prions) and how they cause disease; transmission and vectors; Koch's postulates; innate and adaptive immunity; antibodies, B and T cells; vaccination and herd immunity; epidemiology and controlling outbreaks. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 4: Maintaining the internal environment)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Biology worksheets on infectious disease: pathogens, transmission, vectors, the three lines of defence, B and T cells, antibodies, vaccines, herd immunity and antibiotic resistance. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Three lines of defence: barriers, innate response, adaptive response.
key_sub: Memory cells make the second response faster and stronger.
body_html:
How to think about it

Pathogens include viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists, parasites and prions. They spread by direct contact, droplets, food and water, or vectors such as mosquitoes (Ross River virus).

The body's defences: (1) barriers such as skin and mucus; (2) the innate response (inflammation, fever, phagocytes); (3) the adaptive response, in which B cells make antibodies and T cells kill infected cells and make memory cells. Vaccines create memory without disease; high vaccination rates give herd immunity.

Example

R₀ = 3. How many people infected after 3 generations from 1 case?

1 → 3 → 9 → 27

Answer: 27 new cases in the third generation

Example

A newborn gets antibodies in breast milk. Type of immunity?

antibodies made by another person

no memory cells

Answer: natural passive immunity

Common mistakes

  • Using antibiotics for a viral infection.
  • Saying a vaccine contains antibodies: it contains antigens.
  • Thinking people become resistant to antibiotics: bacteria do.

faq.q: What is the difference between active and passive immunity?
faq.a: Active: your own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells (after infection or vaccination). Passive: you receive ready-made antibodies, so protection is short.

faq.q: Why do some vaccines need boosters?
faq.a: Memory cell numbers and antibody levels fall over time, or the pathogen changes (as with influenza), so a booster renews protection.
